n: The council can’t carry out an execution under Roman rule, so the whole group brings Jesus to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor.

f.g: Pontius Pilate, Roman prefect of Judea about AD 26–36, who alone could order a crucifixion.

n: They twist their religious charge into political ones Rome would care about: stirring up rebellion, opposing taxes, and claiming to be a king. The tax charge is plainly false.

f.w: forbidding to give tribute to Cæsar

n: Pilate asks whether He is the King of the Jews. Jesus answers, “You say so” — affirming it, though His kingdom is not the kind Pilate fears.

f.g: An affirmative idiom: “It is as you say.”

n: Pilate declares Jesus innocent — the first of three times in this chapter that he says so.

f.w: I find no fault in this man

n: The accusers press harder, insisting He is stirring up trouble everywhere from Galilee to Judea.

f.g: Judea, or the Jewish homeland generally.

n: Hearing the word “Galilee,” Pilate asks if Jesus is a Galilean — spotting a chance to shift responsibility.

f.g: From Galilee, which was ruled by Herod Antipas.

n: Since Galilee is Herod Antipas’s territory, Pilate sends Jesus to him. Herod is in Jerusalem for Passover. Only Luke records this hearing.

f.g: Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome.

n: Herod is delighted. He has wanted to see Jesus for a long time — but only hoping to be entertained by a miracle.
Herod asks Him many questions, but Jesus says nothing at all. The man who silenced John the Baptist now receives silence from the Word of God.
The chief priests and scribes stand there making fierce accusations.
Herod and his soldiers treat Him with contempt, mock Him, dress Him in a splendid robe as a joke king, and send Him back to Pilate.

f.g: A bright, shining garment — mocking His claim to kingship.

n: That day Pilate and Herod, once enemies, become friends. Their shared contempt for Jesus unites them.

f.w: Pilate and Herod were made friends

n: Pilate summons the chief priests, the leaders, and the people.
He announces that he has examined Jesus publicly and found no basis for their charges.

f.w: touching those things whereof ye accuse him

n: Neither did Herod. Two rulers have now found Him guilty of nothing deserving death.
Pilate proposes a compromise: have Him whipped and then release Him — punishing an innocent man to appease the crowd.
It was customary to release one prisoner at Passover. This verse is missing from some early manuscripts but matches Matthew and Mark.

f.w: of necessity he must release one

n: The crowd shouts together: Away with Him! Release Barabbas to us!

f.g: Aramaic for “son of the father” — ironically, the true Son of the Father is condemned in his place.

n: Barabbas had been imprisoned for leading a riot in the city and for murder. The crowd chooses a rebel and killer over the Prince of Peace.
Wanting to release Jesus, Pilate appeals to them again.
They keep shouting: Crucify Him! Crucify Him!

f.g: Crucifixion was Rome’s most shameful and agonizing execution, reserved for slaves and rebels.

n: A third time Pilate asks what evil He has done, declares he finds no grounds for death, and repeats his offer to flog and release Him.

f.g: Luke emphasizes Jesus’ innocence through Pilate’s three declarations.

n: They persist with loud, relentless shouts demanding crucifixion, and their voices win.
Pilate gives in and sentences Jesus as they demand. Political pressure overrides justice.
He releases the rebel and murderer they asked for and hands Jesus over to their will. The guilty goes free; the innocent dies in his place — a picture of the Atonement.
On the way, soldiers seize Simon from Cyrene in North Africa, coming in from the countryside, and force him to carry the cross behind Jesus — a picture of discipleship.

f.g: From Cyrene, a city in modern Libya with a large Jewish community.

n: A large crowd follows, including women mourning and wailing for Him.

f.g: Beat their breasts and wailed in grief.

n: Jesus, even in His agony, turns to them: Daughters of Jerusalem, don’t weep for Me, but for yourselves and your children. His concern is for them.
Days are coming when people will say childless women are fortunate — so terrible will be Jerusalem’s destruction.
People will beg the mountains to fall on them and the hills to hide them — words from Hosea expressing utter despair.
A proverb: if they do this to green, living wood (the innocent Jesus), what will happen to dry wood (a guilty, ripened-for-judgment nation)?

f.g: Green wood burns poorly; dry wood burns readily.

n: Two criminals are led out with Him to be executed.
At the place called the Skull, they crucify Him between the two criminals — numbered with transgressors, as Isaiah foretold.

f.g: From the Latin calvaria, “skull”; Aramaic Golgotha.

f.w: one on the right hand, and the other on the left

n: Jesus prays for His executioners: Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they’re doing. The JST clarifies He meant the soldiers. Meanwhile they gamble for His clothes.

f.g: JST Luke 23:35 adds: “Meaning the soldiers who crucified him.”

n: The people stand watching. The leaders sneer: He saved others — let Him save Himself if He’s really God’s Messiah. Ironically, He saves others precisely by not saving Himself.
The soldiers mock Him too, offering Him sour wine.

f.g: Cheap sour wine, the common drink of soldiers.

n: They jeer: if You’re the King of the Jews, save Yourself.

f.g: The temptation to come down echoes Satan’s wilderness challenges.

n: A sign above Him reads “This is the King of the Jews” in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew. Meant as mockery, it proclaims the truth to the whole world.

f.g: An inscription naming a condemned person’s crime.
The languages of culture, government, and religion — understood by all present.

n: One of the criminals hanging beside Him joins the insults: If You’re the Christ, save Yourself and us!
The other criminal rebukes him: don’t you fear God? You’re under the same sentence.
We deserve this, he says, but this man has done nothing wrong. Even a dying criminal testifies to Jesus’ innocence.

f.w: the due reward of our deeds

n: Then he speaks to Jesus: remember me when You come into Your kingdom. He sees a King in a dying man.

Jesus promises: today you will be with Me in paradise. Latter-day Saints understand paradise as part of the spirit world, where Jesus went to minister after His death — and where this man would hear the gospel.

f.g: A Persian word for a garden; here the world of spirits after death.

n: From about noon until three in the afternoon, darkness covers the whole land. In the Americas, three days of darkness marked His death.
The sun stops shining, and the temple veil — the curtain before the Holy of Holies — tears in two. The way into God’s presence is opened through Christ.

f.w: the veil of the temple was rent

n: Jesus cries out loudly and prays, quoting Psalm 31: Father, into Your hands I commit My spirit. Then He dies. He gives up His life willingly; no one takes it from Him.

f.w: Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit

f.g: Breathed His last; released His spirit.

n: The Roman centurion in charge praises God and says: surely this was a righteous man. A Gentile soldier confirms His innocence.

f.g: A Roman officer commanding about a hundred soldiers.
Matthew and Mark record him saying “the Son of God.”

n: The crowds who came to watch go home beating their chests in grief and regret.

f.g: A sign of sorrow and repentance.

n: His friends, including the women who followed Him from Galilee, watch from a distance. These faithful women will be key witnesses to the burial and the empty tomb.

f.w: the women that followed him from Galilee

n: A man named Joseph enters the story — a member of the council, good and righteous.
He had not agreed with the council’s decision. From Arimathea, a Judean town, he was looking for God’s kingdom.

f.g: A town in Judea, perhaps the birthplace of Samuel (Ramathaim).

f.w: waited for the kingdom of God

n: He goes to Pilate and asks for Jesus’ body — a courageous act that publicly identified him with the condemned man.
He takes the body down, wraps it in linen, and lays it in a new tomb cut into rock, never before used — fulfilling Isaiah’s words about a rich man’s grave.

f.w: wherein never man before was laid

n: It is Preparation Day, Friday, and the Sabbath is about to begin at sundown. The burial must be rushed.

f.g: The day before the Sabbath, when everything was readied.

n: The Galilean women follow and see the tomb and how His body was placed. They will know exactly where to return.

f.g: Their eyewitness of the burial makes their later witness of the empty tomb credible.

n: They go home and prepare spices and perfumed oils for His body, then rest on the Sabbath as the law commands — even in grief, obedient.

f.g: Aromatic spices and oils used to honor and anoint a body.
